speaker: Kathleen Sullivan
title: Supreme Court and Appellate Advocacy | Kathleen Sullivan
question: During a multi-judge appellate oral argument, how does an advocate escape being trapped by relentless questioning from a hostile judge?
guest: Well, eye contact is the key to oral argument, and you want to make sure you're paying attention to all the interlocutors on the bench, not just focusing on some. If you've had a sympathetic question from another judge or justice on your bench, you certainly want to try to quote them by name and get back to them as soon as you can and try to get them to come in and help you.

points.core: Shifting eye contact across the entire bench breaks a hostile judge's monopoly.
points.note: Accept: visually engaging all judges on the panel rather than locking eyes exclusively with the adversarial questioner so friendlier judges feel invited to speak. Do not credit: generic advice to make eye contact or stay polite.

points.core: Quoting a sympathetic judge's earlier question by name invites them to intervene.
points.note: Accept: explicitly referencing a friendly judge by name to pivot back to their point and prompt them to jump in as an ally. Do not credit: generic advice to pivot back to your own talking points.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The core technique is to answer the hostile judge's question directly and briefly, then pivot away rather than keep fighting on that judge's ground. You are arguing to the whole panel, and you only need a majority, not that one vote.

In practice, give a straight answer first ("Yes," "No," or "No, because…"); evasion costs you credibility with the other judges. If the point is one you can safely concede, concede it and explain why it doesn't decide the case. Then bridge immediately to your strongest argument, widening your eye contact to the other judges as you do: "But the dispositive point here is…"

If the judge keeps pressing, don't repeat the same exchange. Acknowledge the disagreement respectfully ("I understand Your Honor's concern, and I may not persuade the Court on that point, but we prevail regardless because…") and move on. Watch for a friendly question from another judge; it is often a deliberate lifeline, so take it and build on it.

Throughout, stay calm and courteous, never interrupt, and never show irritation. Composure under hostile fire is itself persuasive to the rest of the bench.

models.answer: To escape relentless questioning from a hostile judge, an advocate must first resist the urge to evade or grow defensive, since dodging a question only invites sharper follow-ups. Instead, give a crisp, direct answer—conceding nonessential points if helpful—and immediately bridge back to an affirmative theme. Because appellate victory requires a majority rather than unanimity, use the exchange to persuade the quieter, undecided judges listening on the bench, tailoring your answers to the limiting principles and record facts they need. Physically break the one-on-one lock by beginning your response looking at the questioner, then expanding eye contact to the rest of the panel, which widens the conversation and subtly invites a colleague or the presiding judge to step in with a new question. If the hostile judge still will not let go, respectfully acknowledge the disagreement and pivot with an "even if" transition—showing why your client prevails on an independent ground even under that judge's premise—to move the argument forward gracefully.

noweb.answer: To escape relentless questioning from a hostile appellate judge, an advocate must first resist the urge to evade, since dodging questions only prolongs the grilling and alienates undecided panelists. Begin with a direct "yes," "no," or qualified answer, immediately pairing it with the limiting principle or record fact that protects your client. Readily concede extreme hypotheticals or peripheral points you do not need to win, which defuses the judge's momentum. From that answer, pivot smoothly back to your core affirmative argument, ideally referencing a concern raised earlier by another panelist to invite other judges back into the conversation. Throughout, stay composed and use the hostile judge's questions as vehicles to persuade the silent majority watching the exchange. If an impasse persists as time winds down, respectfully acknowledge the disagreement, offer any narrower fallback ground for ruling in your favor, and ask permission to briefly address your remaining dispositive issue.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Start by answering the question directly. Evasion makes a hostile judge press harder, and the rest of the panel notices. Give a short, candid answer, concede what you honestly have to (a small concession often ends the line of questioning), and show why it doesn't decide the case: "Yes, Your Honor, but even so, the statute's text still controls because…"

After that, bridge back to your main theme instead of arguing the same point again. Remember that you need a majority, not this one judge. If two or three answers haven't moved them, say respectfully that you don't think you'll persuade them on this point, give your best one-sentence answer, and make clear you're moving on: "If I may turn to why that concern doesn't apply here…" As you do, look at the other judges. A sympathetic judge will often step in with a question that rescues you, so treat that question as your opening.

Stay calm and courteous throughout. Never show irritation or interrupt. Most of the escape is built in preparation: anticipate the hardest questions, especially from judges you know are skeptical, and rehearse tight answers and transitions back to your argument.

models.answer:
To escape a hostile judge's relentless questioning on a multi-judge panel, start by answering each question directly, concisely, and without defensiveness. Evasion or arguing back only fuels further follow-ups, whereas a crisp "yes" or "no"—followed by a brief explanation or a narrow, strategic concession—removes the judge's reason to keep pressing. Once you have answered, immediately pivot to your strongest affirmative point rather than lingering on the hostile judge's terrain.

Just as importantly, remember that you only need a majority of the bench, not that judge's vote. Break the one-on-one dynamic by shifting your eye contact to the other panelists as you complete your answer and transition to your core argument. This subtle cue signals that you are addressing the full court and invites sympathetic or undecided judges to step in. If the hostile judge continues repeating the same objection, respectfully acknowledge the disagreement, avoid getting pulled into a circular debate, and move directly to an independent ground for ruling in your favor.

Answer the judge’s question directly, then turn back to the full panel and explain why the answer does or doesn’t change the result. If the judge has identified a point you can concede, concede it and state the narrow ground on which you can still win. For example, “Yes, Your Honor, that would bar relief under the first provision. Our claim rests on the second.”

If the same point keeps coming up, briefly restate your answer and ask, “May I turn to the second issue?” If the judge keeps questioning you, keep answering calmly. When another judge asks a question, take that opening and answer it directly. Your aim is to give the whole panel a clear basis for ruling in your favor.

Answer the judge’s question directly, then use the answer to return to the point the whole panel needs to decide. If the judge offers a hypothetical, acknowledge its consequence and explain the distinction: “Yes, Your Honor, if the record showed notice. Here, the trial court found there was none, and that finding controls the result.”

If the judge keeps pressing the same point, look for the concern your answer may have missed. Address it briefly, then pause and make eye contact with the rest of the panel. A pause gives another judge room to enter. If the exchange has run its course and time is short, ask at a natural break, “Your Honor, may I turn to the preservation issue? It provides an independent ground for affirmance.” If the judge continues, answer courteously. You can keep the panel focused without winning the last word.
